A Million Compiles. One Robot Hour.

The robot succeeded. The contract failed.

Four motion segments ran on observations that were 600 ms old. Repair the Rust gate, rebuild in a fresh workspace, and check what the robot actually does.

Disposable workspaces. Reusable compilation.

Every candidate needs fresh validation. The architecture keeps the temporary workspace separate from the compilation service and retained evidence.

Runner workspace
A fresh Git checkout and Cargo output directory host the candidate. Export the patch and evidence before removing the workspace. The Linux host remains running.
Incredibuild
Cargo builds through ib_console with a rustc profile. The new Rust proof command consumes Build History remote-task counters and cache statistics, rejects incomplete telemetry, and computes ratios only after at least five samples per mode. A completed proof run is still required.
Rust + robosuite
Rust owns the policy, lock-step session, protocol identity, timeouts, evidence, verifier entry point, IB telemetry parser and benchmark gate. Python is retained only as the robosuite / MuJoCo simulator adapter and scripted motion source.
Independent checks
Contract tests and simulator checks execute again. The verifier checks required scenarios, ordered proposal/decision/outcome traces, and the exported executable’s digest. The agent’s own report is not the verdict.

Execution today: EC2-backed Linux workspaces on the Incredibuild grid. Target runner provider: islo. The checked-in workflow does not call islo or destroy EC2 instances.

Observation age and build duration use different clocks

Observation age is simulation time minus capture time. The bridge advances at 20 Hz and requests authorization before each motion segment. A segment can contain several physics control steps. Build duration and protocol timeouts use wall time. This is not continuous control-step supervision.

Rust is the control plane, not a label.

The conference path keeps policy and proof in Rust. The simulator boundary stays narrow and explicit.

Typed safety gate
Proposal, observation identity, simulated stop precedence, timestamp validity and StalePerception are Rust types and deterministic functions.
Lock-step runtime
Rust spawns the simulator adapter, binds one approval to one action and tick, rejects malformed messages, and treats timeout as failure rather than permission.
Build proof
swf-cli parses IB Build History and cache counters, requires remote tasks and parent-warmed hits for every IB sample, then reports medians and ranges.
Python adapter only
robosuite is Python-native, so Python steps MuJoCo and proposes scripted segments. It cannot authorize motion or declare the final verdict.

EC2 proof command: scripts/robot-demo/ec2-agentic-physical-ai.sh <run-id>

A change has to earn its result.

The complete rehearsal retains the failure, applies a bounded candidate patch, rebuilds, and executes the checks on the resulting binary.

  1. Reproduce the failure

    Workspace A builds the seeded gate and records the wrongly permitted stale episode.

  2. Review the change

    Export the work order and base revision. Restrict the candidate patch to the gate implementation.

  3. Rebuild in B

    Remove A’s workspace. Apply the patch to the recorded base in B with fresh Cargo outputs.

  4. Check behavior

    Run the contract tests and full scenario matrix. Export the executable and verify its evidence.

The automated rehearsal uses the reviewed fallback patch by default. An externally produced agent patch can be supplied explicitly; the script does not run an LLM.

Why this matters beyond one cube.

The same loop serves systems research, agent research, and physical-AI work. A behavioral claim is worth exactly as much as the run that reproduces it.

Research iteration
Every experiment gets a fresh workspace, a recorded base revision, and exported evidence. A result that cannot be rebuilt from that recorded base is a screenshot, not a finding.
Agentic AI research
An agent may propose the patch, but an allowlist bounds what it can touch and a protected verifier issues the verdict. A self-reported success is not a result.
Physical-AI readiness
Simulation is where a policy violation is cheap. This run shows a successful lift that still failed its freshness contract — exactly the failure class you do not want to meet first on hardware.
Compilation throughput
Incredibuild is integrated into this loop, and the controlled experiment that would measure distribution and cache reuse now exists in Rust. Until that experiment produces a receipt, the speedup stays unmeasured.

One sample per phase, taken from the archived run with caches uncontrolled. B took 522 ms longer than A. Both records indicate Incredibuild use. These two observations demonstrate that the integration path ran; they establish no speedup and are not a controlled cache or performance measurement.

What the archived evidence contains

The historical run reported 10/10 Rust gate tests and 88/88 checks under the original verifier. Those counts describe that revision, not the strengthened current suite. The repository contains traces, manifests, build timings, and the recorded executable digest. The executable itself is not committed, so a clone cannot independently recheck that historical binary. A new rehearsal exports its own verifiable artifact.

The boundary is part of the result.

This demonstrates Rust contract checks and simulated robot behavior. Cube positions come from simulator state. The 250 ms threshold is an illustrative policy. Physical robots, hardware-in-the-loop, trained vision, continuous emergency-stop supervision, and a measured performance benefit remain outside the demonstrated scope.
